concept.name: Outside bar
concept.definition: A bar whose high exceeds the prior bar's high and whose low falls below the prior bar's low, so its full range engulfs the previous bar's range. Price-action traders read it as volatility expansion and a battle between buyers and sellers, with the close's location indicating which side won; it differs from the engulfing candlestick pattern, which compares only real bodies.
concept.intuition: The market explored beyond both edges of the previous session in one bar, a burst of expanded volatility where both sides were tested and the close reveals the winner.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: High_t > High_{t-1} and Low_t < Low_{t-1}. The close near the high is read bullishly and near the low bearishly, especially at support/resistance; a mid-range close is considered weak. Its wide range makes stop placement and position sizing a central practical issue.
concept.formula: Outside bar when H_t > H_{t-1} and L_t < L_{t-1}.
concept.failure_modes: The wide range forces wide stops, so a single failed trade is expensive; mid-range closes are especially prone to whipsaw. In trendless chop, outside bars frequently mark two-sided stop-runs rather than genuine reversals or continuations.
concept.misconceptions: An outside bar is not identical to an engulfing pattern: engulfing requires only the real body to be engulfed, while the outside bar requires the entire shadow range to be engulfed. Nor is every outside bar a reversal signal; many act as continuation bars within trends.
concept.example: After an uptrend stalls at resistance, a bar trades from a low of 47.50 to a high of 50.50, fully outside the prior bar's 48.00-50.00 range, and closes at 47.80 near its low. Traders read this bearish outside bar as supply overwhelming demand at resistance.

citations.source: Technical-Analysis-Pro, "Inside Bar and Outside Bar: Price Action Patterns for Trading"
